Outcome_variable.extract_value: life satisfaction, positive affect, negative affect
Outcome_variable.evidence_source: [/page/2/Text/5] For adult populations, several studies have reported a correlation between life satisfaction and affective well-being of approximately .3 to .5 (Argyle, 2001; Kahneman & Krueger, 2006). However, no consensus has yet been reached regarding the causal relationship between the two components, and several authors therefore accept the possibility of a bi-directional causal relationship between the two (Fors & Kulin, 2016, p.327).[/page/2/Text/6] Lyubomirsky, King and Diener (2005) clarified that, even if a correlation of around .4 to .5 has been identified in undergraduates (Lucas, Diener, & Suh, 1996), satisfaction is not identical to positive affect, concluding that "we eagerly await the day when a full set of findings based on measures of positive affect, as well as related concepts, is available" (Lyubomirsky et al., 2005, p. 13).[/page/2/Text/8] If we assume SWB to have a hierarchical structure, as suggested by Metler and Busseri (2017) and Busseri (2018), several additional questions arise: Is said structure composed only of one cognitive and two affective components? What is the direction of the effects between the cognitive and affective components?
